# Digest R6 — Moo, *The Letter of James* (PNTC, 2000), James 5:12–20

**Source:** Douglas J. Moo, *The Letter of James* (Pillar New Testament Commentary), 2000  
**Cache file:** `R6-5_12-20.txt` (raw L1531–1635)  
**Scope:** Concluding exhortations — oaths (5:12); prayer, anointing, healing (5:13–18); restoring the wanderer (5:19–20)  
**Established slugs:** [[james]], [[douglas-moo]], [[anointing-healing-james-5]], [[moo-james-pntc]], [[double-mindedness]]  
**Extractor rules:** Quotes + loci only from this range; all interpretive claims attributed to Moo; digests only — no wiki edits.

---

## Claims

### C-R6-001 — Three structural problems at the letter’s end
**Claim (Moo):** At 5:12–20 three interrelated structural problems surface: (1) how the prohibition of vows in v. 12 fits the context (before, after, or isolated); (2) whether vv. 13–18 encourage prayer for spiritual restoration or physical healing, and whether they address a specific problem or give general encouragement; (3) where the closing section of the epistle begins (from v. 7, 12, or 13).  
**Quote:** “There are three interrelated problems. First, how does the prohibition of vows in v. 12 fit into the context? … Second, what are the meaning and function of vv. 13-18? Is James encouraging prayer for spiritual restoration or physical healing? … Third, where should we locate the beginning of the closing section of James's epistle?”  
**Locus:** R6 L1–2

### C-R6-002 — “Above all” marks the epistolary conclusion
**Claim (Moo):** The phrase *above all* in v. 12 marks the beginning of the epistolary conclusion. James wraps up by touching three critical community issues, each involving speech: prohibition of frivolous vows (v. 12); mutual prayer for physical and spiritual needs (vv. 13–18); applying the letter’s teaching to those sinning in the matters he has addressed (vv. 19–20).  
**Quote:** “The phrase above all in v. 12 marks the beginning of the epistolary conclusion. James wraps up his letter by touching on three issues that he considers critical for the community. And each of them involves speech.”  
**Locus:** R6 L3

### C-R6-003 — Against reading “above all” as ranking importance within the letter
**Claim (Moo):** Taking “above all” as an indicator of relative importance within the letter is untenable — James cannot mean that the prohibition of oaths is more important than doing the word, the love command, or submitting to God’s grace. The difficulty of that reading is a chief reason to treat the phrase as primarily a literary/epistolary marker, comparable to Hellenistic letter-conclusion formulas and roughly analogous to Paul’s *to loipon* (“finally”).  
**Quote:** “But can James really mean that the prohibition of oaths is the more important thing he wants to say in the letter? More important than doing the word, than obeying the love command, than submitting to God's grace in Christ? Surely not. … Similar phrases occur in the epistolary conclusions of other Hellenistic letters. And the phrase may function similarly to the common [to] loipon … that Paul uses in his letter endings.”  
**Locus:** R6 L9

### C-R6-004 — Residual contextual weight of “above all”: personal integrity
**Claim (Moo):** Even as a literary marker of the letter’s conclusion, “above all” (*pro panton*) retains some contextual significance: James wants to highlight this prohibition because he sees it as getting at the ultimate issue of personal integrity.  
**Quote:** “while taking the phrase as a literary marker that signals the beginning of the conclusion of the letter, we can probably not remove all contextual significance from the phrase. James wants to highlight this prohibition - probably because he sees it as getting at the ultimate issue of personal integrity.”  
**Locus:** R6 L9

### C-R6-005 — “Do not swear” = oaths, not vulgar speech
**Claim (Moo):** When James says “Do not swear,” he prohibits not coarse or vulgar speech but invoking God’s name (or equivalents) to guarantee the reliability of what a person says — whether reinforcing a past affirmation or binding oneself to future conduct. The verb *omnyo* has this sense throughout the LXX and NT.  
**Quote:** “When James says Do not swear, it is not coarse or vulgar speech he prohibits but invoking God's name to guarantee the reliability of what a person says. A person may take an oath to reinforce the truth of something he has said or to bind himself to a future course of conduct.”  
**Locus:** R6 L11

### C-R6-006 — Scripture does not consistently forbid oaths; Lev 19:12 and James’s Leviticus 19 cluster
**Claim (Moo):** Oaths are by no means consistently forbidden in Scripture: God himself takes oaths; OT law demanded truthfulness to oaths rather than prohibiting them. Lev 19:12 is typical and potentially significant for James, given his use of the “love command” of Lev 19:18 as the heart of “kingdom” law (2:8) and his other ethical issues drawn from Leviticus 19. Concern about devaluation of oaths and “weaseling out” by swearing by less sacred things (cf. Matt 23:16–22) produced warnings against overuse (Sirach, Philo).  
**Quote:** “Oaths, as we may also call them, are by no means consistently forbidden in Scripture. God himself takes oaths. … The OT law did not prohibit oaths but demanded that a person be true to the oath he had taken. Lev. 19:12 is both typical and potentially significant for James. … James makes the ‘love command’ of Lev. 19:18 the heart of his ‘kingdom’ law (2:8).”  
**Locus:** R6 L11

### C-R6-007 — James consciously reproduces Jesus’ Matt 5:34–37 tradition
**Claim (Moo):** Jesus commanded disciples not to swear “at all” (Matt 5:34). Matt 5:34–37 is particularly important for understanding James because it looks as if James is consciously reproducing that tradition; the similarity between the two passages is striking when set side by side.  
**Quote:** “Jesus, as it appears, went even further than this when he commanded his disciples not to swear ‘at all’ (Matt. 5:34). Jesus' teaching in Matt. 5:34-37 is particularly important in understanding James' teaching, because it looks as if James is consciously reproducing that tradition. The similarity between the two passages is striking when they are set side by side.”  
**Locus:** R6 L11

### C-R6-008 — “Yes/yes, no/no” is not a substitute oath in Matthew
**Claim (Moo):** Some argue Matthew and James diverge: Matthew allegedly offers a “substitute oath” (“yes, yes” / “no, no”) while James simply prohibits all oaths. Moo judges it more likely that Jesus in Matthew says the same thing as James: truthfulness should be so consistent that no oath is needed; a simple “yes” or “no” should suffice.  
**Quote:** “Some argue that Matthew and James diverge on one crucial point: Matthew suggests a ‘substitute oath’ - ‘yes, yes’ and ‘no, no’ - while James simply prohibits all oaths. But it is more likely that Jesus in Matthew is saying the same thing as James: our truthfulness should be so consistent and dependable that we need no oath to support it: a simple ‘yes’ or ‘no’ should suffice.”  
**Locus:** R6 L15

### C-R6-009 — Anabaptist total prohibition vs Moo’s mainstream reading (voluntary vs legal oaths)
**Claim (Moo):** Many Christians in the Anabaptist tradition have concluded that James (and Jesus) prohibit all oaths and have refused courtroom and other official oaths. Moo doubts James intends to address official/legal oaths that others ask us to take; the exhortation that “yes” and “no” suffice suggests the issue is the **voluntary** oath taken to insure truthfulness of affirmation or promise. Christians committed to integrity should never *require* an oath.  
**Quote:** “But does James (and Jesus before him) intend to prohibit all oaths? Many Christians in the Anabaptist tradition have concluded that this is the case and have refused by consequence to take oaths in the courtroom or anywhere else. However, it is doubtful that James intends to address the question of official oaths - oaths that others ask us to take for legal purposes. As the exhortation to let our ‘yes’ and ‘no’ suffice for themselves suggests, the issue seems to have been the voluntary oath.”  
**Locus:** R6 L17

### C-R6-010 — Further limitation (only evasive oaths) and Pauline “oaths” — caution required
**Claim (Moo):** Some further limit the prohibition to oaths aimed at avoiding absolute truthfulness (cf. Matt 23:16–22); Paul’s frequent “witness” formulas (e.g. Rom 1:9; 2 Cor 1:23; Gal 1:20) are sometimes cited as indirect support. Moo urges caution: we do not know James’s community situation; there is no evidence of the polemical situation that informs Jesus’ teaching; and Paul’s “witness” formulas may not fit the category of “oath.”  
**Quote:** “They suggest that James intends to prohibit only oaths that have the purpose of avoiding absolute truthfulness. … Indirect support for this further limitation comes from Paul's letters, where he frequently appears to take an oath. … Nevertheless, caution is required. … We therefore have no evidence of the kind of polemical situation that informs Jesus' teaching. And Paul's ‘witness’ formulas may not fit into the category of ‘oath.’”  
**Locus:** R6 L17

### C-R6-011 — Prayer paragraph (5:13–18): typical letter ending + health wish; prayer every verse
**Claim (Moo):** Encouragement to pray is typical of NT letter endings; a concluding “health” wish is typical of Hellenistic letters. James combines the two by encouraging prayer especially for physical ailments. Prayer is mentioned in every verse of the paragraph: for the individual in varied circumstances (vv. 13–14) and the community (v. 16a), with emphasis on the power of prayer from a righteous heart (vv. 16b–18).  
**Quote:** “An encouragement to pray is typical of the concluding sections of NT letters. Also typical of Hellenistic letters in general is a concluding ‘health’ wish. James combines the two by encouraging prayer especially for physical ailments. Prayer is clearly the topic of this paragraph, being mentioned in every verse.”  
**Locus:** R6 L21

### C-R6-012 — Full-circle return to trials (1:2) via “in trouble”
**Claim (Moo):** A more important context for the prayer admonition than a weak link to v. 12 (speech about God) is the community’s trials. The opening question “Is any one of you in trouble?” is lexically tied to the prophets’ “suffering” in v. 10; James thus brings the letter full circle back to the “trials of many kinds” introduced in 1:2.  
**Quote:** “A more important context for the admonition to pray is the trials that the community is experiencing. The opening question of the paragraph, Is any one of you in trouble?, is lexically tied to the reference to the prophets' ‘suffering’ in v. 10. James thus brings us full circle at the end of his letter, back to the ‘trials of many kinds’ that he introduced as a basic community problem in 1:2.”  
**Locus:** R6 L21

### C-R6-013 — “In trouble” has broad application (not only gospel persecution)
**Claim (Moo):** *Kakopatheō* (NIV “in trouble”) can suggest trouble for the gospel’s sake elsewhere (2 Tim 2:9; 4:5), and the noun in v. 10 points that way, but other context elements broaden the meaning: economic oppression by the wicked rich (5:6); Job’s multi-form suffering; and the “weakness” of physical illness in vv. 14–15 as one specific example of “trouble.” Taken together, the word covers trials of all kinds.  
**Quote:** “Taken together, then, the data suggest that the word has a broad application, covering trials of all kinds.”  
**Locus:** R6 L23

### C-R6-014 — Prayer in trouble primarily for endurance, not necessarily removal
**Claim (Moo):** Because *proseuchomai* is general, content of the prayer in v. 13a is uncertain; petition for removal of the trial is possible, but James’s concern with trials elsewhere (1:2–4, 12; 5:7–11) is endurance with a godly spirit and divine historical perspective — so the prayer encouraged is presumably for spiritual strength to endure.  
**Quote:** “Perhaps James would include petition to God to remove the trial. But James's concern when he deals with trials elsewhere (1:2-4, 12; 5:7-11) is to encourage believers to endure the suffering with the right spirit and with a divine perspective on history. Presumably, then, the prayer that he encourages here is for the spiritual strength to endure the trial with a godly spirit.”  
**Locus:** R6 L25

### C-R6-015 — Happiness (*euthymeō*) is emotional state; praise as lifestyle
**Claim (Moo):** The second situation is not the exact opposite of “in trouble”: *euthymeō* (NIV “happy”) connotes an emotional state rather than outward circumstance (cf. Acts 27:22, 25 — “peace of mind” amid storm). A reminder to turn to God is needed even more in cheer than in suffering. *Psallō* here is almost certainly a song of praise to the Lord; present tenses of both “pray” and “sing” indicate regular lifestyle practice.  
**Quote:** “A reminder to turn to God is needed even more in times of cheer than in times of suffering. … So, especially coming from one who is doing well, the song here is almost certainly a song of praise to the Lord. … Giving praise to God, like our petitions for sustenance in times of trouble … should be a regular part of our lifestyle.”  
**Locus:** R6 L27

### C-R6-016 — *Astheneō* in 5:14 = physical illness, not spiritual weakness (overwhelmingly likely)
**Claim (Moo):** *Astheneō* (“to be weak”) can mean many kinds of weakness in the NT; a minority proposes “spiritually weak” here, citing possible spiritual senses of *kamnō* (v. 15), “healed” (v. 16), *sōzō* (“save”), and “raise up,” and arguing the letter’s rebukes of spiritual lassitude fit such an exhortation. Moo holds the usual view (virtually all modern English Bibles) — **physical illness** — is overwhelmingly likely.  
**Quote:** “But the usual view, adopted in virtually all modern English Bibles, that James is speaking here of physical illness, is overwhelmingly likely. When astheneo refers to spiritual weakness, this meaning is made clear by a qualifier … or by the context. More importantly, in the NT material that has exercised the greatest influence on James's vocabulary and theology (the Gospels), astheneo always denotes physical illness.”  
**Locus:** R6 L29–31

### C-R6-017 — Gospel parallels and Mark 6:13 clinch physical sense
**Claim (Moo):** The cluster of terms here parallels physical-healing usage: *sōzō* frequently denotes restoration of the ill in the Gospels; “heal” (v. 16) likewise; and “anointing with oil” occurs only once else in the NT, as a means of **physical** healing (Mark 6:13).  
**Quote:** “The verb ‘save’ is frequently used in the Gospels to denote the restoration of those who are ill … as is, as we might expect, the verb ‘heal’ (v. 16). But perhaps the most striking parallel comes with the reference to ‘anointing with oil.’ Only once else in the NT is the practice mentioned, and then as a means of physical healing (Mark 6:13).”  
**Locus:** R6 L31

### C-R6-018 — Call the elders, not self-pray; elders as pastoral office
**Claim (Moo):** Unlike v. 13’s two situations, the ill believer is not commanded to pray himself but to **call the elders of the church** to pray over him. Elders appear in Acts (Jerusalem and Pauline churches), in the Pastorals, and are assumed by Peter and James; *episkopos* is probably a different title for the same office. Elders were spiritually mature men guiding local congregations; the pastoral function was likely carried out by elders (Acts 20:28).  
**Quote:** “Unlike the first two general situations James mentioned in v. 13, the believer (note one of you) who is ill is not commanded to pray himself but to call the elders of the church to pray over him. … Both Peter (1 Pet. 5:1) and James assume the ministry of elders in the church, showing that the office was well established in the early church.”  
**Locus:** R6 L33

### C-R6-019 — Healing power not confined to charismatics or officeholders alone
**Claim (Moo):** James’s attribution of healing power to elders’ prayer stands out next to Paul’s “gift” of healing (1 Cor 12:9, 28). Early churches differed in gift manifestation; Corinth may be exceptional. Organization channels gifts rather than ignoring them. Elders, recognized for maturity, are natural to call for healing prayer because they should discern the Lord’s will and pray with faith that receives healing — yet James also makes the church at large pray for healing (v. 16a). Without denying a gift of healing, he encourages all Christians, especially those with pastoral oversight, to pray for healing.  
**Quote:** “while not denying that some in the church may have the gift of healing, James encourages all Christians, and especially those charged with pastoral oversight, to be active in prayer for healing.”  
**Locus:** R6 L35

### C-R6-020 — Serious illness implied (summoned; “pray over”)
**Claim (Moo):** Since elders are summoned to the sick person, the sickness is serious enough to restrict mobility. “Pray over” (*proseuxasthōsan ep’ auton*) is unique in biblical Greek for this combination and might picture elders standing over the sick person, or be shorthand for laying hands on during prayer.  
**Quote:** “Since the elders are summoned to the sick person, we may assume that the sickness is serious enough to restrict the mobility of the sufferer. The same conclusion might be suggested by James's use of the preposition over after the verb pray. Only here in biblical Greek does this combination occur.”  
**Locus:** R6 L37

### C-R6-021 — Anointing timing secondary; four interpretive options mapped
**Claim (Moo):** Beside praying, elders are to anoint with oil in the name of the Lord. Timing (aorist participle before vs contemporaneous with prayer) is less important than meaning. Interpretations divide into two main categories with subdivisions: (1) **Practical** — (a) medicinal, (b) pastoral (stimulus of faith/expression of concern); (2) **Religious** — (a) sacramental, (b) symbolic (consecration).  
**Quote:** “But more important than the timing of the act is its meaning: What does James think that the anointing will accomplish? … Interpretations can be divided into two main categories, with subdivisions in each.”  
**Locus:** R6 L39–41

### C-R6-022 — Medicinal option stated (oil as ancient remedy)
**Claim (Moo):** Oil was widely used as skin conditioner and medicine (e.g. Luke 10:34; Galen on oil as remedy for paralysis). On this view elders come with both spiritual and natural resources — prayer and medicine — both administered with the Lord’s authority.  
**Quote:** “Considering this background, we might suppose that James is urging the elders to come to the bedside of the sick armed with both spiritual and natural resources - with prayer and with medicine. Both are administered with the Lord's authority, and both together can be used by him in healing the sick.”  
**Locus:** R6 L47

### C-R6-023 — Pastoral-practical option (props to stimulate faith)
**Claim (Moo):** As another practical purpose, anointing may have been an outward physical expression of concern and a means to stimulate the faith of the sick person; Jesus sometimes used physical props in healings with such a purpose.  
**Quote:** “As a different kind of practical purpose, others suggest that the anointing may have been intended as an outward, physical expression of concern and as a means to stimulate the faith of the sick person. Jesus sometimes used physical props in his healings, apparently with just such a purpose.”  
**Locus:** R6 L49–51

### C-R6-024 — Sacramental option: Euchelaion / extreme unction vs James’s text
**Claim (Moo):** Early Greek church practiced *Euchelaion* (prayer + oil) to strengthen body and soul of the sick; the Roman church later developed extreme unction (A.D. 852), with Trent finding the sacrament “insinuated” in Mark 6:13 and “promulgated” in Jas 5:14; since Vatican II, “anointing of the sick.” Moo: this developed sacrament has little basis in James’s text — he recommends anointing for **any** illness and associates it with **healing**, not preparation for death. A thinner sacramental reading could still treat oil as a “vehicle of divine power” analogous to the Lord’s Supper conveying grace.  
**Quote:** “Clearly this developed sacrament has little basis in James's text: he recommends anointing for any illness and associates it with healing rather than with preparation for death. Nevertheless, the oil could have a sacramental function in that it acted as a ‘vehicle of divine power.’”  
**Locus:** R6 L53–57

### C-R6-025 — Symbolic-consecration option (OT/NT anointing as setting apart)
**Claim (Moo):** Anointing frequently symbolizes consecration of persons/things for God’s use in the OT (e.g. Exod 28:41) and continues as metaphor for consecration in the NT (Luke 4:18; Acts 4:27; 10:38; 2 Cor 1:21; Heb 1:9). If James has this background, elders anoint to show vividly that the person is set apart for God’s special attention in prayer.  
**Quote:** “If James has this background in mind, then he would be recommending that the elders anoint the sick person in order vividly to show how that person is being set apart for God's special attention in prayer.”  
**Locus:** R6 L59–61

### C-R6-026 — Lexicography (*aleiphō* vs *chriō*) does not settle the options
**Claim (Moo):** James uses *aleiphō*, not *chriō*. In LXX/NT, *chriō* regularly designates consecration (and in NT never a physical act); *aleiphō* most often marks cosmetic/hygienic anointing, with some ceremonial LXX uses (Exod 40:15; Num 3:3). Neither word has medicinal significance in Scripture (Luke 10:34 uses *epicheō*). One could argue James would have used *chriō* for symbolic consecration — but *aleiphō* was the only word available for an actual physical anointing act. Lexicography does not definitely rule any of the four options in or out.  
**Quote:** “Lexicography does not, then, definitely rule in or out any of the four main options.”  
**Locus:** R6 L61–65

### C-R6-027 — Moo’s choice: physical action with symbolic significance (consecration)
**Claim (Moo):** Other factors suggest James probably views anointing as a **physical action symbolizing consecration**. Positively, that is by far the most common symbolic significance of anointing in the Bible. Negatively: (1) medicinal view — oil not evidenced as remedy for every medical problem, and why only elders if purely medical (others would already have applied it); (2) pastoral can be incorporated but value is not physical connection of action to malady as with many of Jesus’ healing gestures; (3) sacramental conveyance of healing grace conflicts with v. 15’s insistence that healing comes through “the prayer of faith.” As elders pray, they anoint to symbolize that the person is set apart for God’s special attention and care.  
**Quote:** “But other factors suggest that James probably views the anointing as a physical action symbolizing consecration. … We conclude, therefore, that ‘anoint’ in v. 14 refers to a physical action with symbolic significance. … As the elders pray, they are to anoint the sick person in order to symbolize that that person is being set apart for God's special attention and care.”  
**Locus:** R6 L65–67

### C-R6-028 — Anointing not confined to apostolic age; not necessary for every healing
**Claim (Moo):** Calvin, Luther, and others confine anointing (and healing power) to the apostolic age; Moo: such temporal restriction cannot be established. Recommendation that regular church officers carry it out implies permanent validity. Conversely, mention only here among NT epistles and many healings without anointing show it is not a necessary accompaniment to prayer for healing.  
**Quote:** “Calvin, Luther, and other expositors think that the practice of anointing, along with the power to heal, was confined to the apostolic age. But such a temporal restriction cannot be established. James's recommendation that regular church officers carry out the practice would seem to imply its permanent validity in the church. On the other hand, the fact that anointing a sick person is mentioned only here in the NT epistles, and that many healings were accomplished without anointing, shows that the practice is not a necessary accompaniment to the prayer for healing.”  
**Locus:** R6 L67

### C-R6-029 — Prayer is main concern; *euchē* / “prayer of faith” subordinate oil
**Claim (Moo):** Anointing attracts attention because unclear, but is clearly subordinate to prayer — James’s main concern. V. 15 picks up the elders’ prayer from v. 14; *euchē* (elsewhere “vow” in Acts 18:18; 21:23) here with its cognate verb’s sense of fervent petition. This prayer, when offered in faith, will make the sick person well; the Lord will raise him up.  
**Quote:** “Anointing with oil, because its significance is so unclear, attracts a lot of attention in this passage. But anointing, whatever it signifies, is clearly subordinate to James's main concern in these verses: prayer. … This prayer, James affirms, when offered in faith, will make the sick person well; the Lord will raise him up.”  
**Locus:** R6 L69

### C-R6-030 — *Sōzō* / *egeirō* / *kamnō* = physical healing, not dual spiritual sense
**Claim (Moo):** *Sōzō* usually means “save” and is spiritual elsewhere in James (1:21; 2:14; 4:12; 5:20); some want spiritual (or dual physical+spiritual) sense here. Moo rejects: salvation is never the result of prayer in the NT; giving two meanings to “save” and “raise up” violates the semantic principle of not giving a word more meaning than the context requires. Physical restoration is all the context requires. Gospel usage of *sōzō*, LXX *kamnō*, and *egeirō* in healing stories support physical raising from the sickbed.  
**Quote:** “A physical restoration is all that the context requires, and we should be wary of adding an unnecessary reference to spiritual deliverance. Several elements of the text require a reference to physical healing; everything in the text makes sense as a description of physical healing. … Thus the picture is of the elders praying ‘over’ the sick person in his bed and the Lord intervening to raise him up from that bed.”  
**Locus:** R6 L69–71

### C-R6-031 — “If he has sinned”: possible link of sin and illness, not assumed
**Claim (Moo):** The conditional “if he has sinned, he will be forgiven” might seem to favor spiritual interpretation, but actually reinforces physical healing: sin and sickness were often associated in the ancient world; Job and Jesus (John 9:2–3) show a direct illness–sin link is impossible to assume, yet the NT recognizes some illnesses as products of sin (Mark 2:1–12; 1 Cor 11:27–30). The *kan* (“if”) is doubly important: James does **not** assume sickness is caused by sin; and it makes pure spiritual-weakness readings hard, since spiritual “weakness” hard to imagine without sin.  
**Quote:** “The ‘if’ (kan) is therefore doubly important: it shows that James by no means assumes that sickness is caused by sin; and it makes a spiritual interpretation of the passage difficult, since it is difficult to imagine a condition of spiritual ‘weakness’ that would not be a product of sin.”  
**Locus:** R6 L71

### C-R6-032 — Apparently unconditional promise: not solved by apostolic-age confinement or eschatological-only healing
**Claim (Moo):** The promise “the prayer offered in faith will make the sick person well” appears unconditional. Confining healing power to the apostolic age has no textual basis. The view that God may heal now but will infallibly “heal” at the resurrection (*egeirō* as resurrection language) is theologically appropriate but robs the text of its point: eschatological healing needs no special elder visit or anointing — it is part of salvation itself. James envisages a much more immediate result.  
**Quote:** “this interpretation, though theologically appropriate, robs the present text of its real point. Believers who struggle with illness can, indeed, be confident that God will heal them in the end. But it does not require a special visit from the elders nor an anointing with oil to accomplish that. … James plainly envisages a much more immediate result of this special time of prayer for the sick believer.”  
**Locus:** R6 L73

### C-R6-033 — “Enough faith” critique: devastating double burden is unbiblical
**Claim (Moo):** Fruitful approach focuses on qualification: only the prayer **offered in faith** brings healing (echoing 1:6 on asking without doubt). Certain preachers insist a believer needs “enough faith” to be healed — resulting in a devastating double burden: remaining illness plus assumption of insufficient faith. Moo: this is profoundly unbiblical. Moreover, in James the prayer of faith that heals is offered by the **elders**, not the sufferer — so the “enough faith” burden would fall on them, which poses the same problem.  
**Quote:** “Certain preachers and writers make a great deal of this call for faith, insisting that a believer simply needs to have enough faith in order to receive healing from the Lord. The devastating result of this line of thinking is that believers who are not healed when they pray must deal with a twofold burden: added to their remaining physical challenge is the assumption that they lack sufficient faith. But this way of looking at faith and its results is profoundly unbiblical. And, in James, at least, the prayer of faith that heals in v. 15 is offered not by the sufferer but by the elders (v. 14).”  
**Locus:** R6 L75

### C-R6-034 — Faith in sovereign will; God does not always will to heal; van der Loos
**Claim (Moo):** Faith in prayer is faith in the God who sovereignly accomplishes his will; usually prayers for healing must be qualified by recognition of God’s supreme will. God does not always will to heal (Paul’s thorn, 2 Cor 12:7–9; Trophimus left sick, “Titus 3:20” in Moo’s text — 2 Tim 4:20 standard reference). Faith sometimes includes assurance that a particular request is within that will, but such cases are rare. Parallel: John 14:14 “in my name” means taking Jesus’ will into account. Prayer for healing offered in confidence that God will answer brings healing — but only when it is God’s will to heal will that faith (itself God’s gift) be present. Citing H. van der Loos: faith, forgiveness, and healing are dispensations of grace, their relations governed by God’s will, not causality.  
**Quote:** “The faith exercised in prayer is faith in the God who sovereignly accomplishes his will. … A prayer for healing, then, must usually be qualified by a recognition that God's will in the matter is supreme. And it is clear in the NT that God does not always will to heal the believer. … Prayer for healing offered in the confidence that God will answer that prayer does bring healing; but only when it is God's will to heal will that faith, itself a gift of God, be present. As H. van der Loos puts it, ‘faith, forgiveness and healing are all three in essence dispensations of the grace of God. This implies that the relations between these three are not governed by the law of causality but by the will and intention of God.’”  
**Locus:** R6 L77

### C-R6-035 — V. 16 *therefore*: mutual confession/prayer as conclusion of physical-healing discussion
**Claim (Moo):** “Therefore” marks mutual confession and prayer as the conclusion readers should draw from vv. 13–15. On Moo’s physical-illness reading of 14–15, best is to take “that you may be healed” (*iaomai*) physically: v. 16 concludes the specific healing discussion — confession (because sin can sometimes cause illness) and prayer so that physical healing in the community can take place. *Iaomai* when used independently in the NT always applies to physical malady (exception Heb 12:13, where sin is already compared to sickness).  
**Quote:** “This last interpretation, tying v. 16 closely to the discussion of physical healing in vv. 14-15, is probably best. For the verb heal (iaomai) is consistently applied to physical afflictions. … When used independently, as here, it always is applied to a physical malady.”  
**Locus:** R6 L79–81

### C-R6-036 — Confession to each other: only explicit NT command; sins hindering healing; whole body prays
**Claim (Moo):** This is the only NT verse that explicitly commands believers to confess sins to one another (basis for eighteenth-century Methodist “rule” for small meetings). Context of healing suggests sins that may have caused the illness for which prayers are offered, rather than only confessing to those directly harmed (cf. Matt 5:25–26). Important shift: v. 14 elders pray; now the **whole church body** prays. Per Davids (quoted by Moo): James “consciously generalizes, making the specific case of 5:14-15 into a general principle of preventive medicine.” Power to heal is invested in prayer, not the elder office.  
**Quote:** “This is the only verse in the NT that explicitly commands believers to confess their sins to one another. … We should note an important shift in emphasis in the passage: in v. 14 the elders are encouraged to pray for healing; now, however, the whole church body is to pray. As Davids says, James ‘consciously generalizes, making the specific case of 5:14-15 into a general principle of preventive medicine.’ … the power to heal is invested in prayer, not the elder.”  
**Locus:** R6 L83

### C-R6-037 — Prayer of a righteous person: every believer, not super-saints; *deēsis* petitionary; middle not passive “energized”
**Claim (Moo):** The “righteous man/person” is simply the believer, righteous by receiving forgiveness through Jesus; prayer is powerful in the hands even of the humblest believer. Third Greek prayer word here is *deēsis* (petitionary). NIV “powerful and effective” renders adverb + verb + participle; passive “when energized (by God/Spirit)” would subtly qualify effectiveness by God’s energizing — theologically attractive but probably reads too much in; participle is probably middle, “as it powerfully works.”  
**Quote:** “The righteous man, or ‘person’ … is simply the believer. … Prayer, James wants to make clear, is a powerful weapon in the hands even of the humblest believer; it does not require a ‘super saint’ to wield it effectively. … However, as theologically attractive as this interpretation might be, it probably reads too much into the text. The participle is probably a middle, with the sense ‘as it powerfully works.’”  
**Locus:** R6 L85

### C-R6-038 — Elijah example: *homoiopathēs* “just like us”; drought prayer; tradition fills OT silence
**Claim (Moo):** Elijah illustrates the powerful prayer of a righteous person. James is interested not in Elijah’s prophetic endowment or unique place but that he was “a man just like us” (*homoiopathēs*; cf. Acts 14:15). Elijah “prayed earnestly” (Semitic cognate construction) for drought and later for rain (1 Kings 17–18); OT does not state he prayed for the drought’s onset, but 1 Kgs 18:42 pictures prayer for its end, and onset prayer is a legitimate inference. James’s three and a half years (cf. Luke 4:25) specifies the rounded “three years” of 1 Kgs 18:1 — perhaps with symbolic judgment associations (Dan 7:25; Rev). Why this illustration rather than Carmel fire or the widow’s son? Analogy between sick believer restored and dead land revived is not strongly drawn; James partly relies on Jewish tradition associating drought with Elijah’s praying (Sir 48:2–3; 2 Esdr 7:109).  
**Quote:** “But it is not Elijah's special prophetic endowment or unique place in history that interests James, but the fact that he was a man just like us. … Although the OT does not state that Elijah prayed for the drought, 1 Kgs. 8:42 does picture him praying for the drought to end, and it is a legitimate inference to think that he prayed for its onset also. … Probably, then, James at least partly relies on Jewish tradition, where there is evidence for an association between the drought and Elijah's praying.”  
**Locus:** R6 L87–91  
**Note:** Moo’s printed “1 Kgs. 8:42” in this range is the verse he cites for Elijah praying for the drought’s end; standard parallel is 1 Kgs 18:42 — record as Moo’s reference in-range without correction in claim voice.

### C-R6-039 — 5:19–20: sermon-like ending; intervene for those failing the letter’s demands
**Claim (Moo):** James does not end with greetings/benedictions but with a summons to action — more typical of formal “sermon-like” NT letters (1 John a close parallel). Fitting, given James’s density of imperatives: the community is to intervene on behalf of fellow Christians struggling with the spiritual matters James has discussed.  
**Quote:** “James does not conclude his letter with greetings and benedictions typical of epistolary endings, but with a summons to action. This kind of ending is more typical of the more ‘formal’ NT letters that read like published sermons; 1 John is an especially close parallel. … So it is fitting that he would in the end turn to the community with an encouragement to intervene on behalf of fellow Christians who may be having difficulty with the spiritual matters that James has been discussing.”  
**Locus:** R6 L95

### C-R6-040 — “Wander from the truth”: gospel as done + believed; serious deviation / apostasy-level
**Claim (Moo):** “Truth” is not Christian doctrine in a narrow sense but all involved in the gospel — to be done as well as believed (Ps 51:6; Gal 5:7; 1 John 1:6). For James, correct doctrine cannot be separated from correct behavior; mind, mouth, and body must align — anything less is worldly, sinful “doublemindedness” (1:8; 4:8). *Planaō* (“wander”) is not limited to inadvertent/casual sins; given that v. 20 saves the wanderer from spiritual death, the deviation is very serious, tantamount to apostasy. “Bring back” (*epistrephō*) here is restoration of one of the community who has outwardly identified as Christian, not initial conversion.  
**Quote:** “The truth does not refer here to Christian doctrine in the narrow sense, but more broadly to all that is involved in the gospel. This truth is something that is to be done as well as believed. … What the mind thinks, and the mouth confesses, the body must do - anything less is worldly, sinful ‘doublemindedness’ (1:8; 4:8). … since James suggests in v. 20 that the ‘wandering’ Christian is saved from spiritual death, the deviation from the faith here must be a very serious one, tantamount to apostasy.”  
**Locus:** R6 L97–99

### C-R6-041 — “Save him from death”: spiritual/eternal death of the restored sinner
**Claim (Moo):** Result of successful intervention: whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save him from death and cover a multitude of sins. “Death” here, as commonly in James and almost always in the NT where sin is the issue, is ultimate spiritual death — condemnation to eternal damnation from unforgiven sin (cf. *thanatos* in 1:15). Turning the sinner back “saves” his life; spiritual *sōzō* elsewhere in James (1:21; 2:14; 4:12) contrasts with physical sense argued for 5:15.  
**Quote:** “‘Death’ here, as commonly in James and almost always in the NT where sin is the issue, is ultimate ‘spiritual’ death - the condemnation to eternal damnation that results from unforgiven sin. … when he is turned back from that journey, he has ‘saved’ his life.”  
**Locus:** R6 L101

### C-R6-042 — Whose soul saved / whose sins covered: primarily the restored sinner
**Claim (Moo):** Greek leaves somewhat ambiguous whose “soul” is saved and whose sins are covered. The referent of the pronoun after “save” is almost certainly the converted sinner (not the converter). “Cover” alludes to Prov 10:12; in 1 Pet 4:8 the phrase became traditional for God’s forgiveness of sins. Many interpreters encourage the converter with hope of forgiveness for his own sins (cf. Ezek 3:21; 1 Tim 4:16; treat-others theme in Matt 6:14–15; James 2:12–13) — Moo allows James may well so encourage. **But** sequence of thought makes it awkward to refer covering of sins to a different person from the one whose salvation is described; Scripture often pairs salvation with covering/blotting of sins as parallel. **Probably**, then, both end-of-v. 20 descriptions refer to spiritual benefits enjoyed by the **sinner who is turned from his sin**.  
**Quote:** “While it is possible to understand the ‘soul’ that is saved to be that of the person who does the converting, the referent of the pronoun him after save is almost certainly the sinner who has been converted. … Probably, then, James refers to the spiritual benefits enjoyed by the sinner who is turned from his sin in both descriptions at the end of v. 20.”  
**Locus:** R6 L103

### C-R6-043 — Closing pastoral logic: do the word and see that others do it; eternal death motivates
**Claim (Moo):** If James is a sermon in epistolary form, 5:19–20 are an appropriate conclusion: readers should not only “do” what James has written but be deeply concerned that others “do” them also. Sharing James’s conviction that there is eternal death to which the way of sin leads motivates dealing with sin in our own lives and others’.  
**Quote:** “Not only should the readers of James ‘do’ the words he has written; they should be deeply concerned to see that others ‘do’ them also. It is by sharing with James the conviction that there is indeed an eternal death, to which the way of sin leads, that we shall be motivated to deal with sin in our lives and in the lives of others.”  
**Locus:** R6 L105
